title: Fascism is the heroin of political ideologies
subtitle: Deleuze and Guattari on fascism and liberalism
author: Jacob McNulty
introduction: The term fascism is being thrown around a lot in political debates at the moment. The focus tends to be on the ideology of fascism, as far-right, authoritarian, and ultranationalist, characterized by dictatorial power and the suppression of opposition. But Yale philosopher Jacob McNulty argues fascism is not persuasive because of its ideas. It works more like heroin: genuinely enjoyable for those caught up in it, but destructive in the end, and very hard to give up. Drawing on Deleuze and Guattari, McNulty argues that liberal moral condemnation of this ideology has proven a dead end because it refuses to reckon with fascism's appeal. Understanding this requires liberals to do something difficult — inhabit the desires of people they deplore. Fascism is exciting and genuinely revolutionary... that's exactly what makes it so dangerous.
body:
When academics try to understand fascism, they rarely stop to consider how fun it is for its adherents. Deleuze and Guattari’s Capitalism and Schizophrenia is an under-utilized resource for understanding this resurgence of right-wing politics. It cautions against over-intellectualizing political phenomena, like in the classical Marxist theory of ideology, where social forms are partly upheld by belief systems. Instead, Deleuze and Guattari draw on Spinoza for an alternative model that prioritizes affect, the body and experience. This alternative model suggests the gaudy forms of entertainment endorsed by Trump and his followers, i.e. pro-wrestling or MMA, should be central, not peripheral, to our analysis. It also implies a connection to addiction and other pathological forms that the American “pursuit of happiness” takes. Ultimately, though, Capitalism and Schizophrenia is valuable for the unexpected way in which it reinforces a classic Marxist thesis concerning fascism: “whoever is not willing to talk about capitalism should keep quiet about fascism.”

The F-word is back—and in a big way. Consider the “fascism debate,” a recent academic dust-up over whether, and to what extent, Trump is fascist. It drew contributions from scholars and authors of diverse persuasions, often pitting ultra-leftists and Marxists against more conventional liberals. Neither group, of course, wanted to exonerate Trump. Still, the hard left worried that deeming Trump a fascist would make him a kind of historical anomaly, and in so doing excuse the Democratic party’s backslide into plutocracy and cronyism. The center left shot back with reminders of the very real racism, misogyny and authoritarianism of the Trump movement, further provoking the ire of those who viewed the Trump phenomenon through the lens of neo-liberalism and its evisceration of America’s middle class.

Deleuze and Guattari can address one of the fascism debate’s blind spots: its neglect of just what a rollicking good time right-wing movements are for those caught up in them.

Those interested in the debate may wish to consult Danny Steinmetz Jenkins’ edited volume, Did It Happen Here? Perspectives on Fascism in America. But, to make a long story short, each camp was partially vindicated by Trump’s second term. The movement has now revealed itself to be openly racist, misogynistic and xenophobic; it is contemptuous of the rule of law, free markets, and other pillars of the liberal order; it now embraces military expansion. Yet as the hard left stressed, the pathologies of Trump are clearly inseparable from neoliberal capitalism and its contradictions. If the rust-belt’s rightward turn didn’t quite confirm this, the presence of Bezos et. al. at the Trump inauguration does. So, when it comes to the fascism debate, it turned out that everybody was a winner. Or maybe we all lost, since, in a way, the threat turned out to be stranger and scarier than either side realized. Now the academy itself is under threat. And that means the possibility of no more edited volumes, about this or anything else.

Some of the main protagonists in the fascism debate were theorists and philosophers, and they often invoked the great thinkers of the past: Marx, especially the 18th Brumaire; the Frankfurt School; the black radical tradition; Chomsky and Howard Zinn; and others. Here, I want to suggest that we have something to learn from Deleuze and Guattari, a pair who, so far as I know, were never invoked in the course of the debate.

Their writings, “theory” classics like Capitalism and Schizophrenia and A Thousand Plateaus, are closely associated with the student upheavals of May ’68, the anti-psychiatry of R.D. Laing, and, of course, a project known as “the marriage of Marx and Freud” (fusing Marxism and psychoanalysis to understand contemporary society). Yet Deleuze and Guattari were also perceptive theorists of fascism, theorists in the lineage of Wilhelm Reich and Spinoza (who memorably observed that those who are oppressed desire submission as if it were salvation).

So far, the fascism debate has limited itself to a small set of interlocutors, but Deleuze and Guattari can address one of its blind spots: its neglect of just what a rollicking good time right-wing movements are for those caught up in them.

The first and most striking feature of Deleuze and Guattari’s analysis is their abandonment of the category of ideology, which they understand as overemphasizing the role of false beliefs, ignorance or insufficient knowledge. In their view, the primary task is to understand why fascism is desired, often by people who are in no way deluded about what it entails. Their hero is Reich, who suggested that the masses desired fascism, though they chide him for remaining within the Freudian paradigm. They also hearken back to Spinoza, who sought to understand how people could desire subordination as if it were their own salvation.

Unlike Reich, Deleuze and Guattari are, as announced in the title of their master-work, anti-Oedipus, anti-Freudian: more specifically, they are opposed to the idea that we erotically invest in tyrants, kings, bosses and others only because they are reminiscent of fathers. For Deleuze and Guattari, no projection of the father onto these figures is necessary. The erotic (libidinal) investment of leaders is direct, not indirect, and it happens all the time. Or perhaps one could say that there is nothing special about the father. We love his power and the pleasure it promises, but we can have this orientation toward other figures in the social world, too. And, of course, the power of the father has a legal, political and economic dimension that even children discern. In rejecting ideology critique and instead probing desire, Deleuze and Guattari in effect ask us to consider not how those caught up in right-wing movements think, but how they feel; not how they come to be convinced or persuaded, but how they come to be seduced or incited.

As an analogy, think of a rather cerebral philosopher-type attempting to understand why people become addicted to heroin, and zeroing in on their irrational beliefs: “I can kick the habit any time!” “Present pleasures outweigh future harms.” Those false beliefs may play some role. Yet a lot would be clarified for our observer by simply trying the drug and discovering its potency and addictiveness. The analogy is not incidental. Deleuze and Guattari were interested in addiction and viewed it as a “destructive line of flight” (a type of rebellion against society which is ultimately self-defeating for the one mounting it). Surprising as it may sound, fascism turns out to share addiction’s logic.

Privileging desire over belief may seem like an over-correction or worse. It may seem like it threatens to make us less effective critics of our political opponents. Arguments get resolved, but there may (in the end) be no accounting for taste. However, the old adage is exaggerated. Taste can be criticized. Fascism, like heroin, does not tend to end well for the majority of its adherents, even if it can be quite durable and destructive. A desire-based approach allows us to appeal to our opponent’s self-interest, not just their morality.

__

Of course, it may be too late for any type of appeal. But, barring that, one that appeals to emotion, affect and feeling might just do the trick. Certainly, the moralistic scolding that characterized the liberal commentariat during Trump 1 proved a dead end. Approaching fascism as Deleuze and Guattari do demands something difficult of us. It demands that we inhabit the desires of a group of people we deplore (“deplorables”). This requires overcoming not just moral compunction but more visceral forms of aversion and disgust.

Trumpism is more than a political movement. As Andrew Breitbart preached, “politics is downstream of culture.” Trump himself rose to prominence on reality TV, a genre few academics or scholars consume; his rallies are as important as his arguments; his chief of staff comes from the world of pro-wrestling, a milieu with many Trumpian resonances; and many of his closest collaborators and enablers are part of the mixed martial arts community, one of the fastest growing forms of sport and entertainment. Yet the cultural antecedents of Trumpism are probably invisible to most academics and scholars. So long as ideology-critique is our aim, they will remain so. We need an analysis of desire. Deleuze and Guattari would agree with Horkheimer’s adage “he who would talk about fascism, must talk about capitalism.”

To understand why fascism is desired, then, we must begin with its relationship to capitalism. For Deleuze and Guattari, capitalism is a system defined by a double-movement: the unleashing and recapturing of “flows.” Capitalism unleashes flows because it is a system that ruthlessly eliminates arbitrary impediments to the free movement of labor, capital, goods and services, cultural products, etc. It wants them to circulate, not stagnate.

Psychologically speaking, it wants desire to circulate too. It not only encourages spending, investment and consumption, but the unconscious and conscious desires that “fund” this economic activity. It also stimulates and promotes erotic desire. This too should flow freely across the social body. To do this, capitalism decodes and deterritorializes these flows. It decodes because it eliminates any classification of things that would obstruct their movement. It wants Romeo and Juliet to marry, even though they are from rival clans. It deterritorializes because it eliminates most geographic restrictions. “Go west, young man!” it says to enterprising workers.

All previous societies simply code and territorialize flows, classifying them and limiting their circulation. Kinship rules are an example, as is the restriction of commerce. People are literally tattooed or branded, and markets are circumscribed. Not much changes even when we go from the savage-barbarian mode of life to the feudal one. Only capitalism knows the power of unleashing flows. We buy what we want, marry who we love, and transact or invest with whomever we please.

However, the unleashing of flows is just one tendency in capitalism (as it were, the boom part of the boom and bust cycle). The other is their recapture. No sooner has capitalism unleashed flows when it realizes it has gone too far and must recode or reterritorialize them. Romeo and Juliet may—indeed must—marry. Henceforth, they must keep their desire confined to monogamous marriage in the nuclear family. Workers, goods and services, and capital circulate, but only up to a point. National borders, for example, may remain impermeable. Or, if they are pierced, there may be a crackdown (like a “big beautiful wall” or the idea of “fortress Europe”). And, of course, booms are often followed by busts. Crises.

Deleuze and Guattari admired Keynes and advocated the integration of his conception of finance capitalism and the business cycle with Marxism. For them, Keynes’s “animal spirits,” basically his term for investors’ exuberance, is as important as the Marxian cycle M-C-M* (spending money to make money, using it to buy a commodity which is then resold at a higher price).  Interestingly, Deleuze and Guattari even regard the logic of unleashing and recapturing flows as pertaining to language. In capitalism, signs circulate more freely than ever before, as modernism in literature attests. Yet they also undergo new forms of subordination to social imperatives.

Capitalism gives rise to a language that is purely functional, consisting in orders or commands that do not need to be understood to be obeyed. Bosses, generals and bankers speak this language, but it can also be found in the code of a computer program. We are a long way from the captured and territorialized speech and writing of earlier societies. Now, fascism is no ordinary recapture or reterritorialization of flows. It is, rather, a departure from the cycle of unleashing and recapturing flows that characterizes business-as-usual capitalism. For Deleuze and Guattari, the threat of racism, misogyny, lawlessness, and authoritarianism is present in capitalism. Yet the threat takes a particular form: the reflux to the flux, the recapture of a flow, the reterritorialization of something fugitive and ungovernable.

SUGGESTED READING East of Eden, free will, and rewriting the myth of your life By Noah Lazarides

Under capitalism, the forces of reaction exist, but they are like brakes we pump when our vehicle accelerates too quickly. Under capitalism, the ordinary racism, misogyny, authoritarianism, and lawlessness are primarily inhibitory. Not so under fascism. Under fascism, the forces of reaction become excitors. They are not brakes that get pumped, but a new kind of engine. The usual rhythm of capitalism is that flows are unleashed and then recaptured. Fascism collapses these phases in such a way that reaction and revolution coalesce. The bitter pill for liberals to swallow is that fascism is genuinely revolutionary, just not in the way liberals want. “Move fast and break stuff” is the motto of the Silicon Valley startup and its left-libertarian members. But nobody moves faster or breaks more than Trump, so that the tech executives bend the knee when the time comes.

Obviously, tightening border security is a form of recoding or reterritorialization, a reflux to counter the flux. However, it has another more excitatory side. In ICE, it functions as a job-creation program for unemployable thugs. They now have an opportunity to vent their sadism on the vulnerable, or at least to experience the rush of handling sophisticated military hardware. It is economically and psychologically empowering for some, even as it imposes new strictures on others. Similarly, tariffs reterritorialize, putting the brakes on global trade. But they also unleash flows of aggression toward an international cosmopolitan elite and a rule-based international order. They promise to unleash flows of desire dammed up amidst the drought of “good jobs.”

Then there is right-wing internet culture and its comic stylings, the Holocaust jokes and Hitler memes of the Republican junior staffers’ group chat that was recently leaked to the public. Does this style of comedy undermine order, because it subverts political correctness? Or does it restore order, because it reinforces racist and misogynistic norms? Obviously, it does both. Or just consider the grim combination of excitation and inhibition found in Nick Fuentes’s tweet issued after the Dobbs ruling: “your body, my choice, forever.”

Capitalism’s cycles of flux and reflux are disorienting and inspire the search for alternatives. Fascism is one. Liberals have trouble conceding this because they consider themselves the real subversives. Yet they must face the uncomfortable truth that their progressivism usually extends only as far as capitalism’s interest in unleashing flows allows. To the extent the far right has this analysis of liberal hypocrisy, it is correct. Understanding why fascism is desired does not entail endorsing it.

In the end, fascism is what Deleuze and Guattari call a destructive line of flight, not a constructive one—not unlike hard drugs themselves. Fascism’s potent combination of flux and reflux exhausts itself quickly. Neither the tariffs, nor the job-creation program for thugs, nor Fuentes’ “Groypers” and their neo-Nazi memes are sustainable long-term, even if they feel good (for some) in the moment. Protectionism and welfare-through-warfare are not sound economic policy, and edgy envelope-pushing humor is not the foundation of a culture. Even in erotic terms alone, fascism cannot compete with the cycles of license and inhibition that sustain business-as-usual capitalism. These cycles built the modern world. Taken to its logical extreme, fascism’s combinations of flux and reflux lead its adherents to desire their own creative destruction: specifically, to welcome their own sacrifice in war.

When I try to imagine American life after Trump, I think about an ex-addict at Thanksgiving. He refuses the beer or glass of wine that is offered, but relishes the meal. He has not recoiled into asceticism. He takes his pleasures where he can, but in a responsible way. The pursuit of happiness is his right, as it is the right of every American. What Deleuze and Guattari remind us is that any such compromise is fragile. Not because turkey cannot compete with heroin, but because that is not actually the choice our society offers us. Our society is constantly inciting us to pursue more potent pleasures, only to reverse course and suddenly demand renunciation. As long as we have this boom-and-bust cycle, there will be the temptation of collapsing the two phases into one. The whiplash of the tennis-match spectator gives way to the focused stare of the Twitch streamer—before he breaks into peals of cruel laughter.
